analysis.one_liner: Toughens workplace safety law with mandatory safety programs, worker committees, higher penalties, and coverage for public employees.
analysis.headline: The Senate labor committee approved the bill and put it on the calendar, but the Senate killed it by unanimous consent on October 8, 1992 — it never got an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the nation's workplace safety law. Every employer would have had to run a written safety program, and employers with 11 or more workers would have had to set up joint worker-management safety committees with paid time for committee work. It would have extended federal safety protections to state, local, and federal government workers for the first time, set deadlines for issuing standards on toxic exposures and ergonomics, raised fines and prison terms for willful violations that kill or injure workers, and protected employees who report hazards or refuse dangerous work from being fired.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary workers, including the millions of public employees then excluded from federal safety law. They would get joint safety committees with the right to inspect worksites, new rights to refuse work that poses an imminent danger without losing their jobs, faster agency action on toxic exposure limits, a required ergonomics standard for repetitive-strain injuries, and rights for injured workers and their families to participate in enforcement. Construction workers would get mandatory site safety plans and certified safety coordinators on large projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, including public employees and construction crews

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA coverage to federal, state, and local government employees, who were previously excluded from the Act [S2][S3].

Requires employers with 11 or more workers to establish safety and health committees with employee representatives who can conduct quarterly worksite inspections, review injury records, and recommend corrections — all on paid time [S2][S3].

Sets statutory deadlines for the Labor Department to issue standards on toxic exposure limits, exposure monitoring, medical surveillance, and a first-ever ergonomics standard for musculoskeletal injuries, and lets courts force the agency to act when it delays [S2][S3].

Increases criminal penalties for willful violations causing death from up to six months to up to 10 years in prison, and creates new criminal penalties for willful violations causing serious bodily injury, including for officers and supervisors [S2][S3].

Protects workers from being fired for reporting injuries or unsafe conditions, extends the window to file a discrimination complaint from 30 to 180 days, and lets workers refuse duties posing an imminent danger once a hazard notice is posted [S2][S3].
Requires every employer to carry out a written safety and health program for identifying and correcting hazards, investigating injuries, and training employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers bear the cost: written safety programs, committee time for workers at full pay, training, exposure monitoring and medical surveillance programs, and an ergonomics program. Employers face fines of $10,000 to $50,000 per day for continuing exposure to posted imminent dangers, higher civil and criminal penalties, and personal liability for executives whose fines can no longer be paid with company money. The Labor Department would need more inspectors and staff, and state and local governments would have to meet OSHA requirements for the first time.

drawbacks.text: Every covered employer must build and maintain a written safety program, fund committees, training, exposure monitoring, and medical surveillance — a real compliance cost, particularly for small businesses [S2][S3].

The bill layers statutory deadlines on an agency already behind on rulemaking, and lets courts order the agency to issue rules it has missed, which backers of slower, more flexible regulation argued could produce rushed or poorly tested standards [S2][S3].

Fines of $10,000 to $50,000 per day for exposure to a posted imminent danger, plus criminal exposure for supervisors, raise the stakes for employers in ways they argued could be disproportionate for ambiguous hazards [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to a broad group — anyone who works — while the costs fall on employers and show up mainly in safety spending that the bill's authors argued prevents injuries and deaths that already cost the economy in medical bills, lost wages, and compensation [S4]. The main good-faith objection is compliance burden and the risk of rigid statutory rulemaking deadlines, but the reported version moderated some of this: it stretched the final-rule deadline from 180 days to 18 months and added an employer defense excusing citations when the employer trained and equipped workers and enforced safety rules the workers ignored [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The Senate labor committee approved the bill with an amendment and put it on the Senate calendar in early October 1992, but two days later the Senate — without anyone objecting — indefinitely postponed it, which set it aside, and it never came up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Kennedy on August 1, 1991 and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S6].
The committee held hearings through 1991 and 1992 and on September 16, 1992 ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S6].

The reported version added a full construction-safety title creating an Office of Construction Safety, project safety coordinators, and site safety plans, and softened some enforcement terms, including an employer defense for violations caused by employees ignoring enforced work rules [S3].
The committee reported the bill on October 3, 1992 with a written report, and additional and minority views were filed — a sign of disagreement within the committee [S6].
On October 8, 1992 the Senate indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent, setting it aside without any recorded vote [S6].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died without a floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the compliance costs, higher penalties, and personal criminal liability are better off because the bill died; workers, including public employees, kept the weaker safety protections that were in place before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing new mandates and penalties

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors and the sponsor were Democrats, no Republicans signed on, and minority views were filed with the committee report [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill imposes written safety programs, joint committees with paid worker time, exposure monitoring, and fines up to $50,000 per day for ignored imminent dangers. Industry's interest in avoiding these mandates runs against the workers the protections are for, though employers also gain from fewer injuries.

The reported version adds a construction-safety title requiring project constructors, certified safety coordinators, written site safety plans, work stoppage authority, and inspector qualifications requiring five years of construction experience — all direct costs to contractors and project owners.

Extending OSHA to public employees puts state and local governments under federal safety rules for the first time, a cost to them that delivers the same protections to their workers as to private-sector employees.
